region: Widespread in South America east of the Andes; Trinidad
description: The classic bronze cory, recorded from Trinidad and Venezuela south to the Río de la Plata; it is really a complex of near-identical species, now placed by some authors in Osteogaster. Pairs spawn in the corydoras "T-position", the female carrying eggs in her cupped pelvic fins to stick them on glass or leaves.

A long-established captive-bred albino of the bronze cory that lacks dark pigment, so the body is pinkish-white with red eyes. It behaves and breeds exactly like the wild form and is one of the most widely sold corydoras.

A uniformly sooty-black aeneus-group cory sold as "Black Venezuela", with only a faint greenish sheen. Whether it began as a wild population or as a melanistic line selected in captivity is unclear; virtually all fish in the trade are captive-bred and behave like the bronze cory.

An undescribed member of the bronze-cory group (now often placed in Osteogaster), catalogued in the CW series as "Gold Laser" for the vivid orange-gold stripe along its dark metallic flank. It forages in groups and spawns in the T-position like its relatives.

The "horseman" cory of the central Brazilian Amazon (described from Codajás), an aeneus-group species named for the orange band that crosses the head behind the eyes like a rider's sash, above a large saddle-shaped dark green-brown patch on the flank. It is rarely exported and is kept like the bronze cory.

A rust-orange member of the bronze-cory group with a matt black band that starts at the dorsal fin, runs back along the top of the body and turns down across the tail stem. It forages in loose groups in clear forest streams of the upper Amazon.
Very like C. rabauti, but its dark band along the upper flank has a metallic green sheen and ends on the tail stem without turning down across it. Native to Peruvian tributaries of the upper Amazon.

An aeneus-group cory from a few tributaries of the Río Meta in Colombia: the upper half of the body is metallic green below a pale yellow back ridge, a green mask crosses the eyes and the fins are yellow-ochre. Its name means "black band"; it is kept and spawned like the bronze cory but is rarely exported.

An aeneus-group cory from northern Venezuela, warm orange-bronze with its dark greenish colour confined to a large oval patch on the shoulder rather than a full-length band. In the trade it is easily confused with orange-toned bronze cory forms sold as "Venezuela orange".

region: La Plata basin & coastal rivers of southern Brazil, Uruguay & Argentina
description: The peppered cory of the La Plata basin, one of the first aquarium catfish ever spawned in captivity (in Paris in the 1870s). It tolerates cooler water than most corydoras and spawns readily after a cool water change.
A captive-bred albino of the peppered cory, pinkish-white with red eyes and only ghostly traces of the mottled pattern. Produced commercially in large numbers and as hardy as the wild type.
A line-bred peppered cory with greatly elongated dorsal, pectoral and tail fins, developed by hobby breeders. The long fins make it a slower, less agile swimmer than the wild form.

Sterba's cory is dark grey-brown covered in white spots, with bright orange leading rays on the pectoral and pelvic fins. A warmth-tolerant species from the Rio Guaporé that is often chosen as a companion for discus.

A captive-bred albino of Sterba's cory: cream to pale yellow with faint pale spots, red eyes and the species' orange pectoral spines still present. It needs the same warm, soft water as the wild form.
A Rio Guaporé cory close to C. sterbai but with the pattern reversed: dark spots on a light golden-tan body, plus orange pectoral spines. Named after the explorer and collector Harald Schultz.

The blue cory of Brazil's Atlantic coastal rivers, silvery blue-grey with a dark band along the middle of the flank from behind the head to the tail. It prefers slightly cooler, well-oxygenated water than Amazonian corydoras.

The slate cory is almost uniformly slate- to blue-grey, lacking the spots and bands of most relatives ("concolor" means one colour), with a rusty-orange tinge to the fins. It is known only from western tributaries of the Orinoco in Venezuela.
Gosse's cory has a plain grey body set off by bright orange fins. It comes from the Mamoré drainage on the Brazil–Bolivia border and was named for the ichthyologist Jean-Pierre Gosse.

region: Coastal rivers of northeastern Brazil (Piauí & Maranhão)
description: The true julii cory comes from coastal rivers of northeastern Brazil and is far rarer in shops than the three-stripe cory often sold under its name. It has clean black spots on the head, where C. trilineatus has a maze of lines.

region: Upper Amazon, Peru, Ecuador, Colombia & Brazil
description: The three-stripe cory of the upper Amazon has a maze of dark lines over the head and back and a black stripe along the flank. Most "julii cories" in shops are actually this hardy, readily spawned species.

The first corydoras ever described (by Bloch in 1794, from Suriname): a pale grey-tan body evenly dotted with fine black spots and a black blotch on the upper part of the dorsal fin. It is rarely exported.

Named after the Río Ampiyacu (formerly "Ambiyacu") in Peru, this spotted cory has sparse, brownish spots, a dark bar through the eye and a black blotch at the base of the dorsal fin that reaches only about halfway up the fin. It is one of several near-identical spotted species from the upper Amazon that are often mixed in imports.

Agassiz's cory is spotted like its upper-Amazon relatives, its larger black spots tending to form rows, with a black mark on the upper flank below the dorsal fin that extends up the first rays of the fin. It is named after the Swiss-American naturalist Louis Agassiz.

The blackfin cory has a spotted pale body, a dark bar through the eye and an almost entirely black dorsal fin, which separates it from similar spotted species of the upper Amazon. "Leucomelas" means white-and-black.

A pale, pearly cory from the lower Rio Purus with a black bar through the eye, dark spots that merge into a band along the upper flank toward the tail, and a widened black spot just below the dorsal fin. Usually wild-caught and somewhat sensitive until settled.

region: Guianas: Essequibo basin to French Guiana
description: The black-sail cory ("melanistius" refers to the black dorsal fin) has a pale, finely peppered body, a dark bar through the eye and a black patch running from the front of the dorsal fin down onto the flank. It lives in clear, sandy streams of the Guianas and was described from the Essequibo River.

The reticulated or mosaic cory is covered in a fine dark net pattern and carries a large black blotch in the dorsal fin. Described from the lower Amazon at Monte Alegre, it is imported mainly from Peru, often alongside the very similar C. sodalis.

Its name means "companion", for its close resemblance to the reticulated cory: it has the same dark net pattern with a darker stripe along the mid-flank, but lacks the black blotch in the dorsal fin. The two are often imported together from Peru.

The violet or smudge-spot cory has a finely dotted head, a greyish body that takes on a violet tone with age and a dark blue-violet smudge covering the tail stem from the adipose fin to the tail. It comes from tributaries of the Rio Madeira in Rondônia and is peaceful and hardy once settled.
As its name says, this Rio Guaporé cory carries a large black spot at the base of the tail on a pale, finely spotted body. An infrequent import that prefers warm, soft water.
The masked cory has bold black spots and a broad black bar through the eyes ("atropersonatus" means black-masked). It is a sought-after but infrequent import from Ecuador and Peru.

A small, pinkish-tan cory endemic to the Río Meta in Colombia (also sold as the pink cory), with one to three dark stripes that begin below the dorsal fin and run back into the lower lobe of the tail. It is named after the aquarium publisher Herbert R. Axelrod.

The bannertail cory from the Rio Aiuanã, a southern tributary of the middle Rio Negro, is the only corydoradine with bold black-and-white horizontal stripes across its tail fin; its silvery-grey body carries rows of black blotches from head to tail. It needs soft, acidic water.

A long-snouted cory densely spotted like a leopard, with a dark stripe on the rear flank and a black-tipped dorsal fin. Like other long-nosed species it probes deeper into the sand than round-snouted corydoras.

region: Upper Rio Negro near São Gabriel da Cachoeira, Brazil
description: Named for the Manaus exporter Adolfo Schwartz, this blackwater cory is creamy white with a black eye mask, a black band along the back and a bright orange patch on the nape. It needs soft, acidic water and is sensitive to poor water quality.

A near-double of Adolfo's cory (its name alludes to this) with a much broader black band along the back and a larger orange nape patch. Like C. adolfoi it comes from soft blackwater streams of the upper Rio Negro.

A Rio Negro member of the adolfoi group: cream with a black eye mask, an orange-red patch on the forehead and a broad dark band along the upper flank. It is named after the ichthyologist Warren E. Burgess.

A long-snouted cory from the upper Rio Negro that copies the pattern of the round-snouted Adolfo's cory living alongside it, one of many corydoras mimicry pairs. The two species forage together in mixed shoals.
The bandit cory from the Río Meta in Colombia has a black mask through the eyes, a black dorsal fin and a black band running along the back to the tail. A hardy, long-popular species.
A long-snouted mimic of the bandit cory from the same Río Meta drainage, with the same black eye mask, black dorsal fin and dark band along the back. Its name means "imitating".

region: Upper Rio Negro & Vaupés drainages, Colombia & Brazil
description: The false bandit cory has a black eye mask and a dark band running diagonally from the dorsal fin down to the lower base of the tail. It lives in the upper Rio Negro and Vaupés drainages of Colombia and Brazil.
"Loxozonus" means oblique band: this Río Meta cory has a dark band slanting from the dorsal fin to the lower base of the tail, over a pale body dotted with small spots.

Named after the catfish author David Sands, this Rio Unini (Rio Negro) cory has the "melini" pattern: a black eye mask and a black band slanting from the dorsal fin to the lower lobe of the tail, with the nape between mask and dorsal fin washed pale orange-red. It prefers soft, acidic water.

The skunk cory has a single black stripe that arcs from the snout over the back and down into the lower lobe of the tail. It is widespread in the upper Amazon and has a long-snouted mimic, C. narcissus.
A large long-snouted cory from the Rio Purus that carries the same arched black stripe as the skunk cory, the classic example of a corydoras mimicry pair. It is only occasionally exported.

The "two-saddle" cory from the Andean foothills of Cusco, Peru: beige with a black eye band, a dark face and two black saddles, a large one below the dorsal fin and a smaller one below the adipose fin, much like a panda cory. Long known only from old museum specimens, it was rediscovered near Quincemil in 2004.

A pale grey-pink cory from the Ucayali basin of Peru with a black eye mask, a black dorsal fin and a dusky band along the back toward the tail. It is imported irregularly with other Peruvian corydoras.

One of the three classic dwarf corydoras: a tan bottom-dweller with irregular dark blotches along the flank and a peppered back. Unlike the pygmy and tail-spot pygmy cories it stays mainly on the substrate rather than shoaling in midwater.

region: Rio Madeira basin, Brazil; also reported from Peru & Ecuador
description: One of the smallest catfish in the hobby, the pygmy cory shoals in midwater among plants and leaf litter instead of staying on the bottom, with a black stripe from snout to tail along its silvery flank. It is now often placed in Gastrodermus.

region: Paraguay basin (Pantanal) & Amazon tributaries, Brazil, Bolivia & Paraguay
description: The tail-spot pygmy cory hovers in loose midwater shoals, sculling with its pectoral fins, and is recognised by the white-edged black spot at the base of its tail. It is now often placed in Gastrodermus with the pygmy cory.

region: Rio Aripuanã drainage (Rio Madeira basin), Brazil
description: A slender dwarf cory from the Rio Aripuanã in the Madeira basin, pale with a single dark stripe that arches from the snout along the upper flank to the base of the tail, a miniature of the skunk cory's pattern. It spends more time swimming in open water than most corydoras.

A small cory from the Rio Guaporé that shoals in midwater like the pygmy species, with a larger eye and more strongly forked tail than bottom-dwelling relatives; its sandy, finely spotted body ends in a blue-black blotch on the tail stem, and the tail fin is banded with rows of spots.

region: Upper Amazon, Peru, Ecuador, Colombia & Brazil
description: A slim upper-Amazon cory that spends much of its time in open water: yellowish with a dark, wedge-shaped band from behind the head to the tail stem above a pale stripe edged below by a row of dark spots, and males carry black bands in the dorsal fin. It gives its name to the elegans group, now often treated as the genus Gastrodermus.

region: Coastal rivers of Suriname & French Guiana
description: A small, active cory from the coastal rivers of Suriname and French Guiana, silvery-cream with three dark lines along the flank. It swims higher in the water than typical corydoras and is regularly bred in aquaria.

A member of the elegans group from the Río Napo, silvery-gold with two or three irregular dark stripes along the flank and a mottled head and back; males carry a black blotch in the dorsal fin. It shoals more actively in open water than typical bottom-dwelling corydoras.

region: Lower Paraná & Uruguay basins, Brazil & Argentina
description: A small cory from the lower Paraná and Uruguay basins whose body is marked with wavy dark lines, as its name suggests. Coming from subtropical waters, it tolerates cooler temperatures like the peppered cory.

region: Coastal rivers of southeastern Brazil (Rio de Janeiro to Santa Catarina)
description: The bearded or banded cory of Brazil's Atlantic coastal streams is one of the largest corydoradines; mature males grow bristly cheek odontodes and a charcoal head with gold markings, including a broad golden streak from between the eyes to the snout tip. It needs cool, well-oxygenated water.

region: Coastal rivers of southeastern Brazil (Espírito Santo to São Paulo)
description: A Scleromystax from coastal rivers of Espírito Santo, Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais and São Paulo, pale with dark spots and blotches and a metallic blue band along the flank; as in its relatives, mature males grow bristle-like odontodes on the cheeks. It lives in clear and whitewater lowland streams.

region: Coastal rivers of São Paulo, Paraná & Santa Catarina, Brazil
description: Mature males of this "big-finned" cory develop a tall, sail-like dorsal fin, long pectoral spines and dense cheek bristles. It lives in cool, often fast-flowing coastal streams of southern Brazil.

A yellowish Scleromystax from Brazil's eastern coastal rivers, densely marked with dark spots; mature males show the genus' bristly cheeks. It was described as Corydoras lacerdai and is still often sold under that name.

A tiny, slender cory with dark irregular spots, dark chevrons toward the tail and a large black spot at the base of the dorsal fin, which has only six branched rays ("pauciradiatus" means few-rayed). Long sold as Aspidoras pauciradiatus, it is a true corydoradine of the elegans group, now placed in Gastrodermus.

region: Coastal rivers of Ceará, northeastern Brazil
description: A small Aspidoras from the coastal rivers of Ceará, sandy-tan with scattered dark spots ("spilotus" means spotted). It is imported only occasionally and is mostly bred by specialists.
Its name means "dark-spotted": a stocky little Aspidoras from Mato Grosso do Sul covered with brown spots. Peaceful and best kept in a group over fine sand.

A small Aspidoras from the upper Rio Tocantins in Goiás, whitish with about four bold, oblique dark bars on the flank ("albater" means white and black). Cave populations with reduced eyes and pigment are known from the São Domingos karst nearby.

region: Upper Amazon, Peru, Ecuador, Colombia & Brazil
description: A large, deep-bodied relative of the corydoras with a long-based dorsal fin of 10–12 rays and an intensely iridescent emerald body; it is sometimes listed as Corydoras splendens. It shoals over soft bottoms in the upper Amazon and gulps air at the surface like corydoras.
The hog-nosed brochis has a long, pointed snout and a very long dorsal fin with 17–18 rays. It comes from the Río Napo drainage of Ecuador and Peru and is imported only occasionally.

The largest brochis, from the upper Paraguay basin, with a long dorsal fin of 15–18 rays and the underside of the head covered by a broad bony shield. It is named after the Brazilian ichthyologist Heraldo Britski.

region: Widespread in South America east of the Andes; Trinidad
description: An elongate, heavily armoured catfish found across most of South America east of the Andes, able to wriggle overland between pools on wet nights. Males build a floating bubble nest under a leaf and guard the eggs.

region: Widespread in South America east of the Andes; Trinidad
description: The hoplo or atipa is a robust armoured catfish of swamps and floodplains that breathes air through its gut and thrives in oxygen-poor water. Males build large floating bubble nests of plant fragments, guard them fiercely and develop thick, reddish pectoral spines in the breeding season.

The port hoplo is a dark, black-spotted armoured catfish with a squared-off tail, living in still, swampy waters of the Amazon, Orinoco and the Guianas. Breeding males develop greatly thickened pectoral spines and a bluish belly, build a floating bubble nest among plants and guard it aggressively.
A slim callichthyid that hovers in midwater in small groups, unlike its bottom-dwelling relatives, sensing food with very long barbels. It builds a bubble nest beneath floating leaves.

region: Lower Rio Negro & central Amazon, Brazil
description: The flagtail porthole catfish is named for the bold black-and-white horizontal stripes on its forked tail. It comes from the central Brazilian Amazon and, like D. longibarbis, hovers in small midwater groups.

region: Paraguay & lower Paraná basins, Paraguay, Brazil & Argentina
description: A small hoplo-like callichthyid from the Paraguay and lower Paraná basins, brown with dark spots and a rounded tail. Males, recognisable by their thickened, milky-white pectoral fins, build bubble nests among floating plants in swampy backwaters and become territorial when breeding.

The true Otocinclus affinis from coastal streams of southeastern Brazil, briefly placed in the genus Macrotocinclus (now a synonym of Otocinclus). It prefers cooler water than Amazonian otos, and most fish sold under this name are actually other species such as O. vittatus.

region: Upper Amazon, Peru, Ecuador, Colombia & Brazil
description: A widespread upper-Amazon oto whose name means "large spot", for the big round black blotch at the base of the tail, separate from the lateral stripe. It is one of the species regularly imported as "common otocinclus".

Described only in 2004 from Peru, the zebra oto is creamy white with bold black blotches that run from the back down to the lower flanks, a dark head and a W-shaped black mark on the tail fin, quite unlike other otocinclus. It needs clean, well-oxygenated water and a steady supply of biofilm.

region: Madeira, Tocantins & upper Paraguay basins and coastal Pará, Brazil
description: A small oto whose dark lateral stripe stops short of a small, separate spot on the tail stem that does not run onto the tail fin. It is often found mixed into shipments of other otocinclus and grazes biofilm from leaves, wood and glass.

region: Upper Paraguay & Madeira basins, Bolivia, Brazil & Paraguay
description: A small oto from Bolivia, Paraguay and Brazil with a broad dark lateral stripe and a mottled back. It grazes biofilm on leaves and glass like its relatives.
A tiny Amazonian oto, olive-brown with a dark lateral stripe, that turns up regularly among imports of other otocinclus. Like its relatives it relies on a constant supply of algae and biofilm.

region: La Plata basin (lower Paraná & Uruguay), Argentina, Brazil & Uruguay
description: A subtropical oto from the La Plata basin with a broad, irregular lateral stripe and a mottled back. It was treated as a synonym of O. flexilis until it was revalidated in 2010, and it tolerates cooler water than Amazonian species.

region: Uruguay & lower Paraná basins, Brazil, Uruguay & Argentina
description: One of the largest otocinclus, from subtropical rivers of southern Brazil, Uruguay and Argentina, mottled brown with an irregular lateral band. It is suited to cooler aquaria than its Amazonian relatives.

region: Río Puré (Colombia) & Amazon tributaries near Iquitos, Peru
description: Described in 2006, this oto is named for the single bat-shaped, W-like black mark on its tail fin, recalling the Batman logo; it also has three dark saddles on the back between the dorsal fin and the tail. It turns up occasionally among otocinclus imported from Peru and Colombia.

The red-fin oto comes from cool, clear coastal streams of southeastern Brazil: mottled golden-brown with darker blotches along the side, red-tinged leading fin rays and a red blotch at the base of the tail ("maculicauda" means spotted tail). Unlike Otocinclus it has a small adipose fin; it needs well-oxygenated water and grazes algae like an oto.

region: Atlantic coastal drainages of southern Brazil (São Paulo to Rio Grande do Sul)
description: A hypoptopomatine from cool coastal rivers of southern Brazil, mottled and faintly striped brown, named ("white-bridled") for the pair of pale yellow lines running from the snout tip to the eyes. It grazes algae and biofilm on plants and stones like an otocinclus and needs well-oxygenated water.

A flattened, broad-snouted relative of the otocinclus whose eyes sit on the sides of the head, visible from below. It grows much larger than otos and likes to cling to thin plant stems and wood in midwater, grazing biofilm while watching around them.
